stature.source: typical: the drafter's figure for the dry Grand Canyon rim, inside Wikipedia's usual 5-15 m and below FEIS's 8-17 m for better sites; tall: 15 m, the Grand Canyon park's own upper figure (NPS); record: about 21 m, Wikipedia's maximum; read 2026-11-10

targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources (2026-11-10), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a short, bushy pine about as wide as it is tall (Wikipedia), a dense, rounded crown nearly to the ground on a short crooked trunk with a few big crooked limbs (FEIS)

pole.note: a young tree under a juniper's shade: a dense, broadly conical bush with thin, scaly, sepia-brown bark

old-growth.note: a tree of several centuries: a thick, crooked trunk of grey, unevenly furrowed bark, a spreading, open, gnarled crown, flattened on top

description: The pine of the pinyon-juniper woodland that rims the Grand Canyon: a short, bushy tree, here usually 4-10 m and about as wide as it is tall, with a rounded, dense crown of short, stiff, upturned needles in pairs on a short, crooked trunk. Its small cones hold big, wingless, edible seeds, the pinyon nuts, which pinyon jays carry off and bury.

season_notes.winter: Evergreen and dark against the snow on the rim; mule deer nibble it a little when other food is short.
season_notes.spring: Small yellowish to red-brown pollen cones shed in late spring.
season_notes.summer: Cones swell through their third summer; resin gives the woodland its sweet pine smell on hot days.
season_notes.fall: In a good year (every few years) the cones open in late September and October and jays, nutcrackers, squirrels and people gather the nuts.

range.where: the pinyon-juniper woodland along both rims of the Grand Canyon and in parts of the inner canyon, below the ponderosa forest; the Colorado Plateau and southern Rockies (Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, Arizona), with outliers to southern Wyoming, Oklahoma and west Texas

notes: A pine grown from ponderosa as a short, wide, round-crowned bush of a tree: a crown about as wide as tall (Wikipedia), a low crown base, a short crooked trunk with a few big crooked limbs and sometimes several stems (FEIS), set here through stems, lean and a thick radius. Needles 2-4 cm (Wikipedia; 1.5-5 cm in FEIS), mostly in pairs, curving upward; Wikipedia calls them blue-green with pale stomatal bands, where the brief described dark yellow-green: the colours here are a dark, slightly grey green between the two and are a judgement, not a measurement. Bark: thin and scaly, sepia-brown when young, grey and unevenly furrowed with age (Wikipedia); the colours are judgement. Cones about 4 cm, nearly round, ripening over three years (FEIS) and not drawn. Elevations: 1220-2280 m in Arizona, lower on north slopes (FEIS); the Grand Canyon rim belt is about 1900-2300 m per the brief. Seed eaters named by FEIS and Wikipedia that are not in the animal library: pinyon jay (the tree's partner and main disperser; NPS Grand Canyon), Clark's nutcracker, Woodhouse's scrub jay (the 'scrub jay' of FEIS; aphelocoma_californica in the library is the coastal species, so it is not used), squirrels and chipmunks; other cover users per FEIS: pronghorn, white-tailed deer, upland game birds. Very sensitive to fire (FEIS). Lives 300-1000 years (Wikipedia, FEIS).
